newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end mostly lower, led by PGMs.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end mostly lower, led by PGMs.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended mostly lower Tuesday, led by further slippage in platinum group metal (PGM) prices, but volumes were very low across the precious metals complex.

"There was some profit taking liquidation by funds in July platinum, and rolling of positions into October, and the squeeze in the physical PGM market has eased a little, but the shortage of metal has not gone away," Credit Lyonnais Rouse New York chief bullion dealer, Scott Mehlman, said.
"Selling to liquidate positions on NYMEX is one thing, but its dangerous to short PGMs without the metal," he said.
NYMEX July platinum ended down $12.20 an ounce at $440.00, as the correction continued from the contract high at $473.80 seen last week.
NYMEX September palladium ended down just $1.10 an ounce at $173.50, after seeing a contract high last week at $186.00.

In the physical PGM market, traders said some leasing activity was being done again at rates around 50 pct for one month, though most dealers had not officially resumed making markets in forwards, but were working customer orders.

Market making in forwards was suspended last week, after the London Platinum and Palladium Market Association met to discuss the acute shortage of metal caused the absence of Russian exports for the past five months.
In overnight news, a Russian Finance Ministry official said Russia's metal export agency, Almaz, should receive a Foreign Trade Ministry licence this week to enable it to resume PGM exports.
Reports Monday suggested the Finance Ministry had held up the licence while it reviewed the Almaz contracts.
Bearish analysts argue the Russians will offer the Japanese and other customers the same amount of PGMs as last year, or options to buy the same amount, when exports resume.
Russian exports of palladium totalled 4.6 million ounces or 67 pct of world supplies last year, and amounted to 1.2 million ounces or 24 pct of platinum supplies.

But bullish analysts argue the Russians will not pack a whole 12 months worth of supplies into the next six months, as fabricators have already secured supplies for the first half of 1997, and the Russians have changed marketing strategy and do not want to force PGM prices back down to early 1997 levels, just to refill the world's inventories.

In addition, hedge fund Tiger Management, believed to have accumulated 1.5 million ounces of palladium, at an average price of $135 an ounce, is seen still holding the metal for a two or three year palladium/platinum convergence play, sources close to the fund said.
Palladium demand is seen rising in the next few years as environmental regulations in the U.S. and Europe encourage more use of PGMs in automotive emission systems.
The amount of palladium used in automotive catalytic converters rose 27 percent to 2.3 million ounces last year, according to a report by refiners Johnson Matthey last month.
Finally, the open positions in Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) palladium, mostly in 1998 delivery months, is equivalent to some 57 tonnes of palladium or 26 pct of 1996 world supply.

"Assuming this is half short, then Japanese brokers have a lot of buying of physical metal to do in Zurich over coming months to square up their books on TOCOM and there isn't much free palladium metal to lend to the market which is why the lease rate is so high," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said in a report.
"So we have three very wild cards," he said. "The Russians, the long U.S. fund, and the behaviour of Japanese brokers and speculators on TOCOM."
Meanwhile, COMEX August gold ended down 20 cents at $346.10, after trading a $346.70-345.40 range.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $343.70/20, compared to the London Tuesday afternoon fix at $343.75 and the New York close Monday around $344.00/50.
COMEX July silver settled up 0.5 cent at $4.745 an ounce.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
